L the Chairmar1 of the Dcparlmcnt.- Rc:lated Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs , having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this Fifth Repor. of the Committ~e. 
2. In pursuanr.:e of the rules relating to the Department-Related Parliamentary 
Standing Committees , the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker , 
Lok Sabha, referred '" The Census (Amendment) Bill, 1992**, as introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on the 18th December, 1992 and pending in that House , to the Committee for 
examination and report. 
3. The Committee in its meeti ngs held on the 18th, 19th and 25th August, 1993 
discussed the provisions of the Bill and also heard the views of the represe:ntative s of 
the Ministries of Home Affairs and Law , Justice & Company Affairs. In its meeting 
held on the 25th August , 1993, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration 
of the Bill. 
In the said meeting the Committee considered and adopted the drafl Report. 
4. ln their background note supplied to the Committee, the Ministry of Home Affair~ 
explained the need for amending the Census At"t, 1948 as follows:-
'The Census is normally taken after every 10 years. The last Census being held in 
1991, the next decennial census would lake place in the year 2001 only. However . 
the Census Organisation is required to undertake surveys or census in parts of the 
country from time to time meet the exigencies of the situation. for example, an 
ethographic survey was done in Jammu & Kashmir in the year 1986-87 to identify 
the communities which should be declared as Scheduled Tribe s. Similarly, in 
Punjab, a survey was done in Kandu Khera village in the year 1986. That is, under 
the Census Act, 1948, census can be taken in any part of the country at any 
particular point of time. Accordingly , it is necessary to get the Census (Amend­
ment) Bill passed as quickly as possible to meet such emergent situations. 
Under the Census (Amendment) Bill, powers are being vested with the Central 
Government to determine the question .naire s for the Census. This power was 
earlier vested with the State Governments ... Different State Governments followed 
different approaches. This not only created administrative difficulties but also, due 
to lack of uniformity, led to uneven quality of data. However , the situation has 
changed drastically in the country during the last three or four decades and it is 
essentia l that there should be uniformity of norms and standards, etc. in the 
censuses and surveys throughout the country. It is towards this end that the powers 
to determine the census questionnaires are being vested with the Central 
Government under the Census (Amendment) Bill ...

Section 7(A) to (H) so as to tackle difficulties faced in acquiring of buildings and 
the vehicles at the time of the Census. The requisitioning of buildings an.-1 vehicles

1, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Fifty-third Report of the Committe~. The Report is on the Immigration 
(Carriers' Liability) Bill, 1998. • 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha 
referred** the Immigration (Carriers' Liability) Bill, 1998 as introduced in the Rajya Sabha 
on the 23rd December, 1998 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and 
report. 
3. The Bill intends to make the carriers liable in respect of passengers brought by them 
into India in contrav entio n of the provisions of the Passport (Entry into India) Act , 1920, 
and the Passport (Entry into India) Rules, 1950. The said Act and the 'rules made. 
thereunder prescribe the conditions for the entry of a person' coming from any place outside 
India by water, land or air. Under these rules, foreign nationals are required to be in 
possession of a valid passport and a visa. An Indian national must be in possession of a valid 1 
passport. The Immigration authorities posted at various checkposts covering land checkposts, 
seaports and airport s are required to do a thorough checking of the persons coming by 
different mpdes of transport. 
4. The Ministry of Home Affairs in their Background Note on the Bill has stated that it 
has been observed in recent years that a large number of passengers at the four major 
Internat ional airports at Delhi, Bombay , Calcutta and Madras manage to come without any 
valid documents, creat ing problems for the immigration authorities. Airlines do not exercise 
proper check of travel documents before allowing passengers to board the plane. It has, 
therefore, become nece~sary that stat utory responsibility is cast on the airlines/ship carriers 
bringing such passengers by imposing financial liability on them, states, the Ministry in their 
Note.· 
5. International air travel is governed by the guidelines adopted at the Convention on 
Internatinal Civil Aviation signed at Chicago on December 7, 1944, known as the Chicago 
Convention. It has various annexures finalised over a period of time during the last 50 years.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised
by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Fifty-fifth Report on the Demands for
Grants (1999-2000) relating to the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions.
2. The Committee heard the concerned officers of the Ministry in its meeting held on 24
th March and 1st April,
1999.
3. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations has mainly relied upon the following :-

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/55_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
i. Presentation made by the concerned officers of the Ministry;
ii. Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry for 1999-2000;
iii. Detailed Demands for Grants of the Union Public Service Commission for the year 1999-2000;
iv. Annual Report of the Ministry for the year 1998-99;
v. Annual Report of Central Bureau of Investigation for the year 1996;
vi. Explanatory Note on the Demands for Grants (1999-2000) received from the Ministry;
vii. Action Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its Forty-forth Report on the
Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Ministry;
viii. Written replies furnished by the Ministry on the Questionnaire sent to it by the Secretariat; and
ix. Written clarifications on the points/issues raised by the Members in the meeting of the Committee.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the
15th April, 1999.
New Delhi PRANAB MUKHERJEE
April , 1999 Chairman
Committee on Home Affairs
REPORT
The management of personnel policies in Government of India, to begin with, was the joint responsibility of the
Ministries of Home Affairs (Services and Establishment Wing) and Finance (Establishment Division) with Union Public
Service Commission playing an important advisory role. The Establishment Officer to the Government of India,
functioning under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under the Government
of India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a unified central didrection.
2. To plug this organisational loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha in its 93
rd Report (April 1966)
observed that "the ever expanding role of the Government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large civil
service calls for effective personnel control through a single agency". The Administrative Reforms Commission too
urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel, to be placed directly under the Prime Minister
to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel functions of the Governm

by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this Fifty-sixth Report on the Demands for
Grants (1999-2000) relating to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs.
2. The Committee heard the concerned officers of the Ministry considered the relevant documents placed before it
and discussed the Demands and other related matters, at its meeting held on 30

REPORT
1. The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs comprises the following Departments :
i. Department of Legal Affairs
ii. Legislative Department,
iii. Department of Justice, and
iv. Department of Company Affairs
1. The main functions of the Department of Legal Affairs are :-
i. To render advice to the various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on legal matters.
ii. To carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government;
iii. To attend to the litigation work in the Supreme Court, High Courts and some of the subordinate
courts;
iv. To handle the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of Civil Law;
v. To authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on behalf of the President
under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution;
vi. To sanction grants-in-aid to certain institutions engaged in research in the field of law.
2.1. The Department of Legal Affairs is further concerned with appointment of the Law Officers, namely the

REPORT
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs having been authorized by the
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present    this Fifty-eighth Report on the Explosive Substances (Amendment) Bill, 1999.
2.         In pursuance of the rule relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in
consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred * the Explosive Substances (Amendment) Bill, 1999 (Annexure-I), as introduced in the
Rajya Sabha on 23 December 1999, and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.         The Bill seeks to amend the relevant provisions of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 by putting more lethal explosives, namely,
RDX, PETN, HMX and other similar explosives or a combination thereof and remote control devices for causing explosion, under ‘Special
Category Explosive Substances’ and to provide for enhancement in maximum punishment for offences committed with such explosive
substances.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
 
RAJYA SABHA
DEPARTMENT-RELATED PARLIAMENTARY
STANDING COMMITTEE ON HOME AFFAIRS
SEVENTY FOURTH REPORT
ON
 
THE CONSTITUTION (NINETY-FIRST AMENDMENT) BILL, 2000
 
(PRESENTED TO RAJYA SABHA ON 26th APRIL, 2001)
(LAID ON THE TABLE LOK SABHA ON 26th APRIL, 2001)
 
REPORT
            The Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Bill, 2000 (See Annexure-I) seeks to amend altogether six Articles of the
Constitution (55, 81, 82, 170, 330 and 332) to remove the distortions and disparities caused due to uneven growth of
population/electorate in territorial constituencies for Lok Sabha/Legislative Assemblies, while sustaining the measure to boost
family planning norms.
1.1              To achieve the foresaid objective, the Bill has the following enabling provisions:-
(i)                  extending the constitutional embargo on undertaking fresh delimitation of constituencies from the year 2000 to
2026;
(ii)                readjustment and rationalization of Parliamentary constituencies in the States without altering the number of seats
allotted to each State in the House of People, including the Schedule Caste and the Scheduled Tribe constituencies,
on the basis of 1991 population census;
(iii)               readjustment and rationalization of Assembly constituencies in the States without altering the number of seats
allotted to each State in their Legislative Assemblies, including the Scheduled Caste and the Scheduled Tribe
constituencies, on the basis of 1991 population census; and
(iv)              refixing the number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the House of the
People and the Legislative Assemblies of the States on the basis of 1991 population census.
2.0       The amendment to the aforesaid seven Articles has been necessitated mainly due to the following two facts:-
(i)                  the constitutional embargo on the delimitation of territorial constituencies (both Parliamentary and Assembly),
imposed by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976, will expire after the publication of first census
after the year 2000 AD, the process of which has already been set in motion; and
(ii)
                the growth of population is not uniform in the country.  The unbalanced and uneven growth of population as well
as continuous migration of people from one place to another, especially from rural to urban areas have resulted in
strikingly different sizes of electoral constituencies even within the State.  The most glaring example is outer Delhi
Parliamentary constituency, which had approximately 29.3 lakhs population whereas the Chandni Chowk
Parliamentary Constituency had a population of 3.7 lakhs (both 1998 figures).
2.1       The last delimitation of territorial constituencies was done on the basis of decennial population census of 1971 by the
Delimitation Commission, constituted for the purpose by the Delimitation Act, 1972 (See Annexure-II).  The Commission took
roughly four years to complete the delimitation work on that occasion, after which the delimitation of Parliamentary and Assembly
Constituencies Order, 1976 came into force. 
2.1.1    The ban on the delimitation was imposed by the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment)Act, 1976 with a specific aim to
boost family planning norms.  It was thought at that time that the States which did not control their population should not get
rewarded through the delimitation process and that by the year, 2000, the progress of implementation of family planning would,
more or less be uniform throughout the country.
2.1.2    But it is found that the population growth since 1971 census is quite haphazard and uneven.  The said uneven growth is

74th Report of Committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/74threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:40:50]
attributed mainly to the fact that some States have gone slow in arresting population explosion whereas some States especially
those in the South have achieved  comparative success in the implementation of family planning programme.
2.1.3    Delimitation on the basis of 2001 population census, in effect, would mean that States which are successful in arresting
population growth to a large extent, would be in disadvantageous position vis-à-vis the States which have gone slow in the
implementation of family planning programme, in the inter-State allocation of seats in the House of the People.
2.2.0    Keeping in view the rationale narrated in the previous para, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has recommended
(See Annexure-III) extending the current freeze up to the year 2026  as by that time the replacement level of fertility would be
expected to be achieved at national level.  In other words, the population growth in the country would be comparatively even by
the year 2026.

INTRODUCTION 
  
 I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Urban Development (2014 -15) 
(Sixteenth Lok Sabha) having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report 
on their behalf, present the First Report on Demands for Grants (2014 -15) of the 
Ministry of Urban Development. 
2. The Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Urban Development were laid on the 
table of the House on 13 th August, 2014. Under Rule 331E of the Rules of Procedure 
and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the Standing Committee on Urban 
Development are required to consid er the Demands for Grants of the Ministries under 
their jurisdiction and make Report on the same to both the Houses of Parliament. 
Thereafter, the Demands are considered by the House in the light of the Report of the 
Committee. However, during the current year, being election year, the demands were 
passed by both the Houses of Parliament without subjecting them to examination by the 
DRSCs. As per directions of the Hon'ble Speaker, the demands have been examined by 
the Committee and reported upon with the in tention that the recommendations of the 
Committee can be utilised by the Ministry for future Demands for Grants. 
3. The Committee took evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Urban 
Development on 17th October, 2014. The Committee wish to express  their thanks to the 
officials of the Ministry of Urban Development for placing before them the requisite 
material and their considered views in connection with the examination of the Demands 
for Grants (2014-15).

December, 2014.

have been printed in bold letters and placed as Part II of the report.

present the Second Report on Demands for Grants (201 4-15) of the Ministry of Housing and 
Urban Poverty Alleviation.  
 
2. The Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation were 
laid on the table of the House on 13 th August, 2014. Under Rule 331E of the Rules of Procedure 
and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the Standing Co mmittee on Urban Development are 
required to consider the Demands for Grants of the Ministries under their jurisdiction and make 
Report on the same to both the Houses of Parliament. Thereafter, the Demands are considered 
by the House in the light of the Re port of the Committee. However, during the current year, being 
election year, the Demands  were passed by both the Houses of Parliament without subjecting 
them to examination by the DRSCs. As per directions of the Hon'ble Speaker, the demands have 
been examined by the Committee and reported upon with the intention that the recommendations 
of the Committee can be utilised by the Ministry for future Demands for Grants.

officials of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Poverty Alleviation for placing before them the 
requisite material and their considered views in connection with the examination of the Demands 
for Grants (2014-15).

PART-I 
CHAPTER- I 
INTRODUCTORY 
 
 (i) Role of the Ministry  
1.1 The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) is entrusted with 
the responsibility of broad policy formulation and monitoring of programmes 
regarding urban housing and urban development. It is the nodal Ministry for 
planning and coordination of urban transport matters at the central level. 
Urban devel opment is a State subject and the Constitution (Seventy -
Fourth) Amendment Act, 1992 has enjoined upon State Governments to 
delegate many functions to urban local bodies.  Government of India, 
however, plays a coordinating and monitoring role and also suppo rts 
various urban housing programmes, urban livelihood mission and overall 
urban development through Central and Centrally Sponsored Schemes. 
The Ministry addresses various issues relevant to urban sector through 
appropriate policy guidelines, subordinate legislation and sectoral 
programmes. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs has f ive attached 
Offices, and three Subordinate Offices, three Public Sector Undertaking s 
and nine Statutory/Autonomous Bodies, including one non -statutory 
registered society and a Government company as shown at Annexure-I.  
 Background 
1.2 Outlining the transformation from rural to urban areas witnessed in 
the country during the last two decades and future requirements to cater to 
ever increasing urban population , the Secretary,(MoHUA) during the 
course of briefing submitted: 
“महोदय , आपने संक्षेप में शुरुआती जो व्याख्यान ददया  है, उसमें आपने बताया 
है दि दिस प्रिार से हमारे देश  में शहरी दििास एि बहुत बड़ी चुनौती िे तौर 

2 
 
पर आगे आ रहा है। दजस प्रिार से शहरों िी आबादी  बढ़ रही है, अगर हम िर्ष 
2001 िे बाद  िर्ष 2011 िे शहरों िी आबादी  देखें  तो उसमें दजस तरह से 
बढ़ोतरी हुई है और जो आगे बढ़ने िा अनुमान है, िर्ष 2011 िी जनगणना िे 
अनुसार शहरी इलािों िी आबादी  िरीब 38 िरोड़ िी थी। इसिा अनुमान है 
दि लगभग  40 परसेंट पॉपुलेशन  यानी हमारी आबादी  60 िरोड़ से ज्यादा िर्ष 
2030 में हो जाएगी। जब िर्ष 2031 िा सेंसस होगा और िर्ष 2051 िी जो 
जनगणना होगी, तब हमारी आबादी  80 िरोड़ से िहीं ज्यादा हो जाएगी, जो 
दि देश  िे 50 परसेंट से ज्यादा यानी हम लोग  आज िी डेट में जो ग्रामीण 
प्रधान देश  िहते हैं, उसिी जगह हम शहरी प्रधान देश  िर्ष 2051 िी 
जनगणना िे बाद  हो जाएँगे। 
सर, शहर हमारे दलए  एि तरफ तो चुनौती लाता  है, उसि े आधारभूत संरचना 
िे बारे में, जैसा आपने िहा सेदनटेशन िे बारे में, िाटर िे बारे में, सीिर 
दसस्टम िे बारे में, दबजली  िे बारे में, क्ोंदि ये तमाम सारे लोग  एि जगह पर 
इिट्ठा होते हैं, उनिो िे तमाम सारी आधारभूत सुदिधाएँ देनी  पड़ती हैं, दजससे 
हम िह िातािरण दिएट िर सि ें, दजससे िे अपनी आदथषि गदतदिदधयों िो 
पूरा िरते हुए देश  िी अथषव्यिस्था में पूरा योगदान  दे  सि ें । 
सर, आज शहरों िा जीडीपी में लगभग  60 प्रदतशत िा योगदान  है। आज 
हमारा जो टोटल  रेिेन्यू है, िह 80 परसेंट से ज्यादा शहरी इलािों से आता है। 
माननीय प्रधान मंत्री जी ने आज देश  िे दििास िे दलए  थ्री दटिदलयन डालर 
इिोनॉमी िो फाइि दटिदलयन डालर इिोनॉमी िर्ष 2024 ति िरने और िर्ष 
2030 ति 10 दटिदलयन डालर इिोनॉमी बनाने िी जो एि चुनौती ली  है, मैं 
समझता हँ दि शहरों िा इसमें बहुत बड़ा योगदान  होगा। मैं आपिो यह भी 
िहना चाहँगा दि िर्ष 2014 िे बाद  से शहरों िे दििास में अभूतपूिष तेजी आई 
है। िर्ष 2014 ति दजस प्रिार से माननीय प्रधान मंत्री जी ने एि िे बाद  एि 
दमशन अप्रोच में बहुत सारी योजनाएँ हमारे मंत्रालय िे दलए  भारत सरिार ने 
स्वीि ृ त िीं और उन योजनाओं िा जो पररणाम सामने आ रहा है, िह उसि े 
दलए  चुनौती है, लेदिन चुनौती िो हम लोग  पूरा िरने िे दलए  एि तरीि े से 
उस रास्ते पर हैं दि ि ै से इसिो पूरा िर सिते हैं।“

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Housing and Urban Affairs (2022-23) having been 
authorized by the Committee, present this Nineteenth Report (1 7th Lok Sabha) on action taken by the 
Government on the Observations/Recommendations contained in the Eighteenth Report (17th Lok Sabha) 
of the Committee on, ‘Demands for Grants (2023-24) of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs’. 
2. The Eighteenth Report was presented to Lok Sabha on 20 March 2023  but had been  laid on the 
table of Rajya Sabha on 17 March 2023 . The Action Taken Replies of the Government to all the 
recommendations contained in the Report were received on 19 June 2023. 
3. The Committee considered and adopted this Report at their sitting held on 01 August , 2023. 
4. An analysis of the  action taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in the 
Eighteenth Report (Seventeenth Lok Sabha) of the Committee is given at Annexure-II. 
5. For the facility of  reference and convenience, the Observations/Recommendations of the 
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

1
REPORT
When India began its long and arduous journey towards industrialisation to foster balanced
economic development, Fabian socialism was adopted as the guiding principle. Pandit Nehru’s
vision was to make India an economic powerhouse with the state owned industrial sector as its
backbone. He considered public sector undertakings as “engines of economic growth.” The
emergence of public sector was expected to play a pivotal role in the economic and industrial
development in the country. India’s economy was then primarily an agrarian economy with a weak
industrial base, low level of savings, inadequate investments and lack of infrastructure facilities. As
such, State’s intervention in all the sectors of the economy was inevitable since private sector
neither had necessary resources, the managerial and scientific skill, nor the will to undertake risks
associated with large long-gestation investments. Considering the gaping inequalities that existed in
the economic and social development, it became a pragmatic compulsion to use the public sector
as an instrument for self-reliant economic growth.

The micro, small and medium enterprises constitute the backbone of our economy. The
buoyancy and dynamism of economic growth and its inclusiveness greatly depend on vibrant and
competitive micro, small and medium enterprises. In fact, some of the developed countries of the
world such as Japan and Switzerland owe their phenomenal economic success to robust medium
and small enterprises which not only provide employment opportunities to vast sections of
population but also significantly boost their exports.
2. In India, the commitment of the Government, particularly the Union Government, to foster
a culture for the growth and expansion of energetic micro, small and medium enterprises was best
demonstrated when a separate Ministry for dealing with such enterprises was created in the year
2007. Mindful of the fact that such enterprises constitute the engine of economic growth and are
at the heart of equitable and inclusive development of economy, the Government has taken several
steps for their onward progress. The numerous benefits of medium, small and micro enterprises in
terms of their employment potential at low capital cost and the scope for greater absorption of labour

having been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this Two Hundred and Thirty-fourth
Report on the Demands for Grants (2012-13) pertaining to the Ministry of Heavy Industries and
Public Enterprises (Department of Heavy Industry).

as the detailed Demands for grants, Annual Report, Outcome Budget, Answers to Questionnaire sent
by the Secretariat and submissions made by the Secretary of the Department and its senior officers
and representatives of select CPSEs & Associations in Auto sector like ACMA, SIAM, FICCI,
ASSOCHAM, CII on 4
th and 9 th April, 2012.
3. The Committee considered and adopted the Draft report at its meeting held on 2 nd May, 2012.
TIRUCHI SIV A

2nd May, 2012 Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry.

1
REPORT
The Department of Heavy Industry deals with many PSEs in the engineering, power and
heavy industry sectors which are critical for nation-building, industrialisation and economic growth.
It also deals with the auto industry which is booming and which has got a lot of potential. Broadly,
the PSEs falling within the following sectors are under the jurisdiction of the Department:–
(i) Heavy Engineering Equipment & Machine Tool Industry (Capital Good Sector);
(ii) H eavy Electrical Engineering Industry; and
(iii) Auto Industry including Tractors and Earth Moving Equipments.
2. DHI aims at ensuring steady growth of all the three above sectors and sub sectors of the
Industry and assists the PSEs in their endeavours to bolster capacity utilization and profitability and
generate resources and reposition their strategies/policies to make them more competitive. The
Department also acts as an interface between PSEs and other agencies for the purpose of long term
policy formulation.

REPORT  
 
The strength of any economy is best reflected in the strength and dynamism of the 
medium, small and micro enterprises.  In our own country, these enterprises constitute the 
mainstay of the architecture of our ec onomy.  These are n ecessary to provide 
employment opportunities to large segments of our population living in far corners of our 
country.  In strengthening and promoting the MSMEs, the culture of inclusive growth is 
promoted.  The significance of the MSMEs can be realized by th e fact that 8 per cent of  
our GDP come from the MSMEs sector.    However, if we look at the percentage share of 
the MSMEs in countries like U.S.A., U.K. and Ch ina, it comes to 40 to 60 per cent.  This 
means that in our country, we have not been able to harness the potential of the MSME 
sector.   
 
2. In the documents supplied to the Committee, it is stated that the vision for 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterp rises is to ensure an orderly and robust 
growth and development of Micr o, Small and Medium Enterpri ses so that these could be

The Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company Limited located  in Tuli in 
Nagaland State is a classic case of a state owned c ompany which became a 
non-starter from its very inception.  The founders of this company 
articulated a bold, forward looking and lofty visio n by stating that it would 
be the market leader in the manufacture of world cl ass eco-friendly paper by 
adopting innovative technologies for sustainable development and to strike a 
harmonious relationship between nature and industry .  Established as a joint 
venture company of the Government of Nagaland and H industan Paper 
Corporation Limited (A Government of India Enterprise) it was incorporated 
on 14 th  September 1971 for production of pulp and paper by  using abundant 
bamboo of the north-eastern region.

estimated at Rs.18.72 crores went up to Rs.83.73 cr ores.  The four fold 
increase in the cost of construction of the project  was indicative of the 
problem of cost overruns which plagued the company and became awe of 
the major factors behind its collapse.

            Foreign investment denotes investment made by a non-resident entity 
in an enterprise in the host country. This can happ en through FDI (Foreign 
Direct Investment) and  Foreign Portfolio Investmen t by FIIs (Foreign 
Institutional Investors) or private equity funds et c.  The FDI denotes foreign 
capital with a longer term perspective and often in vested in productive 
enterprise and may seek managerial control over ent erprise.  Of many other 
modes of getting external finance, FDI is preferred mode due to its long term 
stable nature.  It is less volatile  and does not g enerate or add to debt  
liabilities for the host country. 
 
2. In order to discount unwarranted implications, i n India the FDI flow is 
allowed either through Government route or automatic route. The sectors not 
included in automatic route need Government's appro val and proposals are 
considered by inter-ministerial Foreign Investment Promotion Board under 
M/o Finance or Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion 
(DIPP).  Sectors in which FDI is prohibited include  lottery, chit fund, 
gambling/betting, agriculture and plantation

scheme.  The scheme focuses on the micro enterprise s.

REPORT  
 
BACKGROUND 
 
The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) is a statutory 
body established by an Act of Parliament, 1956, In April 1957, it took over the 
work of former All India Khadi and Village Industries Board. It functions under 
the administrative control of Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises. 
 
2. The statement of objects and reasons of the orig inal KVIC Act, 1956 
states that "with a view to promoting and developing Khadi and Village 
Industries, the Central Govt. constituted a Board called the All India Khadi and 
Village Industries Board and vested it with powers to prepare and organize 
programmes for the production and development of Kh adi and Village 
Industries and to deal with other matters incidenta l thereto.  It has, however, 
been found in actual practice that the work of the 'Board' has been hampered 
by certain procedural and financial difficulties, w hich would be removed if a 
Commission were set up by law.  It is, therefore, p roposed to set up a 
Commission, called All India Khadi and Village Indu stries Commission which 
will be vested with the powers, executive as well a s administrative, for the 
proper development of Khadi and Village Industries.   The bill also provide for 
the All India Khadi and V.I. Board functioning as a n advisory body which will 
advise the Commission generally in the discharge of its duties. “

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Three Hundred 
Twenty-Fourth Report on the subject Promotion of Electric Vehicles in the Country. 
 2.  The Committee took up the subject for detailed examination. As part of 
examination of the subject, the Committee deliberated in detail in its meetings held on 
10th January & 23rd June, 2023, wherein it heard the views of  the Ministry of Heavy 
Industries, Ministry of Power, Ministry of Road, Transport & Highway,  Ministry of 
Petroleum & Natural Gas, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, 
Ministry of New & Renewable Energy, Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue), 
NITI Aayog,  SMEV and during its study visit to various leading EV Manufacturers of 
the Country.  
3.  The Report is based on the submissions made by the Secretaries  & Officers of 
various Ministries; representatives of SMEV and EV Manufacturers; and other materials 
such as Background Notes, Power-Point Presentations and replies to the questionnaires 
submitted to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in 
connection with the examination of the subject. 
4. The Committee express its sincere gratitude to the Ministry of Heavy Industries 
Ministry of Power, Ministry of Road, Transport & Highway,  Ministry of Petroleum &

INTRODUCTION 
 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Three Hundred 
Twenty-Eighth Report on the subject Review of Performance of Prime Minister's 
Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP). 
 
2. The Committee took up the subject for detailed examination. As part of 
examination of the subject, the Committee deliberated in detail and,  
 
i. Reviewed background data and annual reports of the ministry, its official website to 
identify challenges or areas for improvement 
ii. Interacted with officials from the Ministry, key stakeholders like KVIC, public 
sector banks, and beneficiaries 
iii. Circulated detailed questions. 
iv. Conducted study visits to Udaipur (Rajasthan), Mumbai (Maharashtra), Goa, 
Vishakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Kolkata (West Bengal), Srinagar (Jammu 
&Kashmir), Varanasi (Uttar Pradesh), Kochi (Kerala), Chennai (Tamil Nadu), & 
Chandigarh (Haryana- Punjab) ,and 
v. Field visits to identify challenges and areas for improvement. 
vi. Desktop research on Global Data related to MSMEs Sector. 
3. The Committee express its sincere gratitude to the Ministry of Ministry of Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), for placing their valuable suggestions in 
connection with examination of the subject before the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry.

report.

metallurgy of all non ferrous metals both in private and public sectors but excluding Natural Gas , Petroleum

minerals are therefore, of prime importance to the national economy. Besides providing the basic inputs to 
domestic industry the mineral sector accounts for sizeable exports and foreign exchange earni ngs. Having 
regard to the extent and variety of mineral resources in the country there is great potential for rapid growth

CHAPTER–I
MEMORANDUM  OF  UNDERSTANDING  BETWEEN  FERTILIZER  PSUS  AND DEPARTMENT  OF 
FERTILIZERS
1.1       The commitments and mutual responsibilities of the Government and the PSUs are clearly defined in the MoU
System. The targets are finalised at the beginning of the year and so are the commitments of the Department of
Fertilizers. The evaluation of the performance of these targets is carried out only at the end of the year. The focus under
the MoU system hence is said to have shifted from mere input orientation to result orientation. This also envisages a
system granting more autonomy to the PSUs with lesser involvement of the Ministries and Departments in the control of
the day-to-day functioning of the PSUs through laid down procedures etc.
1.2       The Sub-Committee-III on Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises of Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry undertook the study of the MoU System of Madras Fertilizers Limited, Chennai and the
Rashtriya Chemicals and Fertilizers, Mumbai. The Sub-Committee consisted of the following members :

CHAPTER–I
LIQUIDATED DAMAGES – THE CONCEPT
            In a supply contract if there is a delay beyond the contractual delivery period in execution of supply, services,
erection and commissioning, the consignee may end up suffering actual or potential losses. Direct losses arising out of
the delay actual in nature that can be directly quantified like debt servicing etc. Potential losses are indirect losses like
opportunity costs, cost overrun of the project, time overrun of the project leading to inflation of project cost etc. The
losses tantamount to the damages suffered by the consignee and quantified unit of these damages are known as
Liquidated Damages.
2.         As per the standard terms of conditions of contracts internationally acclaimed the amount of liquidated damages
is generally ½% of the total value of the contract for every week of delay in supplies or other performance of the
contract plus any cost escalation that has taken place on account of any increase in taxes or imposition of fresh taxes, or
cost escalation of any raw material on account of this during the period of delay, cost escalation of labour due to any
new wage agreement, or imposition of any statutory conditions. However, the supplier will be entitled to any decrease in
cost on the above account of remission of taxes or withdrawal of taxes during the said period between

          I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred-Seventeenth Report on the Demands for Grants (2003-04)
pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries.
2.       The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry heard the representatives of Small Scale
Industries Associations on the subject on 26th March, 2003 and the Secretary, Ministry of Small Scale Industries on
27th March, 2003.
3.       The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the Draft report
at its meeting held on 6th May 2003.
NEW DELHI;
6 May, 2003
DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
1.1     The Ministry of Small Scale Industries is the nodal Ministry for policy formulation, promotion, development and
protection of Small Scale Industries. It also monitors the implementation of these policies.
1.2     Ministry of SSI designs and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and growth of
small enterprises. The Ministry also coordinates with other Ministries/Departments on behalf of the Small Scale
Industries (SSI) sector.
1.3     Implementation of policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services to
small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organization
(SIDO).
1.4     The Indian economy has experienced profound changes and sustained growth in the last five decades. Industry
sector, by building core strength of the economy, has acted as an engine of growth. The Small Scale Industries (SSI)
sector has also contributed significantly in process of growth and has emerged as a vibrant partner. The importance of
the sector can be well assessed in terms of its contribution to the socio-economic objectives of growth in generation of
employment, output, exports.
1.5     The SSI sector, producing a wide range of products, accounts for around 95 per cent of the industrial units in the
country, contributing to 40 per cent of the manufacturing sector output and approximately one-third of the Nation's

        The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all PSEs and assists in policy formulation
pertaining to the policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel
management and in related areas. It also collects, evaluates and maintains information on several areas in respect of
PSEs. In fulfilling its roles, it associated itself with other Ministries and Organizations.
1.1   The important role and tasks of the Department of Public Enterprises are :
          (i)    General policy relating to Public Sector Enterprises;
          (ii)   Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and Guidelines to Public Sector Enterprises;
          (iii)  Formulation of Policy Guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) in areas like performance
improvement and evaluation, financial management, personnel management, board structures, wage
settlement, training, industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.;
          (iv)  Counselling, training and rehabilitation of employees in Central PSEs under VRS;
          (v)   Matters relating to reservation of posts in PSEs to certain classes of citizens;

1.         The Department of Heavy Industry (Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises) is responsible for promoting
engineering industry in the country and development and growth of capital goods.  The industries covered by this Department
provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport. They also cater to the
requirements of equipment for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping,
paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for the development of  wide range of intermediate engineering
products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gearboxes.  There are 49  Public  Sector Enterprises (PSEs)
under the administrative charge of the Department.
1.1       The PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in manufacturing of engineering/capital goods,
consultancy and contracting activities. The total investment (Gross Block) in 49 Public Sector Enterprises under the Department
of Heavy Industry was about Rs.8234.00 crores till 31st March, 2002,  employing about 1.18  lakh persons.

CHAPTER - I 
MOU SYSTEM 
1.         The Memorandum of Undertaking (MOU)  is a negotia ted document between the Government, acting as the owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific
PSE. It contain the intentions, obligations and mutual responsib ilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MOU makes an at tempt to move the management of PSEs
from management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.  
OBJECTIVES OF THE MOU SYSTEM  
1.1       The objectives of the MOU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy and accountability of the management; to remove the
fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise  to pursue through clearly laid down performance targets   in the  MOU and to enable the evaluation of managerial
performance through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to stimulate improved performance.

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Thirty-second Report on the "MoU performance in respect of PSUs
of Power Sector, Department of Public Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises)".
2.      The Sub-Committee for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises was constituted on the 6th January,
2003. This Sub-Committee has been examining the performance of MoU system in the PSUs and this report deals with
the performance of PSUs of the Power Sector.
3.      The report is based on the deliberations of the meetings held with the representatives of various PSUs and the oral
evidence of representatives of various Ministries at New Delhi on 5th August, 2003 and Chennai on 21st September,
2003.
4.      The Committee at its meeting held on 18th December, 2003 considered and adopted the Report..

CHAPTER-I
MoU SYSTEM
1.      The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a negotiated document between the Government, acting as the
owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific PSE. It contains the intentions, obligations and mutual
responsibilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MoU makes an attempt to move the management of PSEs from
management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.

I, the Chairman, Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry , 
having been authorised by the Committee, present this Fourteenth Report of the Committee 
on the Demands for Grants for 1995-96 of the Ministry of Steel. 
2. The Committee started examination of Ministry's demands by seeking views of the 
representatives of Chambers of Commerce such as FICCI and the CII on the performance of 
the steel sector and the impact of the recent budget proposals relating to Ministry of Steel. 
The Committee also heard the views of representatives of Central trade unions in the same 
context. 
3. At its subsequent meeting held on the 7th April, 1995, the Committee heard oral 
evidence tendered by the Secretary. Ministry of Steel on the Performance Budget for 1995-
96 in connection with the Dema!lds for Grants of the Ministry. 
4. The Committee eonsidered the Ministry's budgetary proposals in three sittings and 
adopted the report at its sittin~ held on the 28th April, 1995. 
S. The Committee was given to understand that the total demand of ~inistry as per 
Demand No. 75 for 1995-96 is to the tune of Rs. 294.46 crore out of which Rs. 284.50 crore 
is for the Plan sector and remaining Rs. 9.96 crore have been allocated to non-plan 
activities. 
6. Taking into account the documents and other material made available to it and the oral 
evidence tendered before it by the representatives of industry. trade unions and the Ministry 
of Steel, the Committee would like to make the following recommendations and suggestions:

budgetary allocations for the Ministry · of Steel for the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96 
would suggest that the allocations are declining steadily over the years. Were the factor of 
inflation to be taken into account, the real content of the outlay proposed for the Ministry 
would appear to be declining at an. even sharper gradient. True, in the ambience of 
liberalisation, the authorities could be influenced by the judgement that the role of the 
government in propelling -industrial growth is going to be progressively less and less from 
now on, justifying cutbacks in the outlays for hithertocrucially important ministries, such as

LEVEL  PLAYING  FIELD  FOR
THE  INDIAN  CAPITAL  GOODS  INDUSTRY
 
CHAPTER - I
IMPACT  OF  FISCAL  POLICY  AND  EXIM POLICY  ON  CAPITAL  GOODS  INDUSTRIES
        In early eighties, when India's economy was on an uptrend, there was need for investment in the infrastructure sector.
Investment from within India was not forthcoming mainly because of higher rate of interest and private sector risk aversions.
Investment during those years was mainly from multilateral/bilateral funding agencies. For judicious usage of these funds, the
projects were established under International Competitive Bidding procedures. Indian companies were also eligible to participate
in the bidding procedure. Overseas suppliers could enjoy soft export financing from their exim banking and other export benefits
prevailing in those countries. The Indian companies were also extended the duty free raw material imports and refund of excise
duty on their finished goods to have a level playing field. Supplies to such projects were termed as Deemed Exports.
        As a part of the commitment given to WTO, the peak rate of customs duty was to be brought down to a level agreed with
WTO in a time bound matter and accordingly the rate of customs duty for the project was also reduced gradually. Project import

linkages in terms of material flow and income generation.   The growth of  many of  advanced economies have been
largely shaped by the strength of their steel industry during their early stages of development.    Some of the newly
industrializing  countries like South Korea, China and Brazil among others have built up substantial capacities not only
to support their rapidly growing domestic economies, but also to export significantly.

REPORT
         The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all central PSEs and assists in policy formulation
pertaining to the role of PSEs in the economy as also in laying down the policy guidelines on the performance improvement
and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel management and in related areas. It also collects, evaluates and maintains
information on several areas in respect of PSEs. DPE also provides an interface between the administrative Ministries and the
PSEs.
2.      The important role and tasks of the Department are listed below:
(i)     General policy relating to Public Sector.
(ii)     Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and guidelines to Public Sector Enterprises.
(iii)    Formulation of policy guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises in areas like performance improvement
and evaluation, financial management, personnel management, board structures, wage settlement, training,
industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.
(iv)    Matters relating to reservation of posts in the public sector enterprises for certain classes of citizens.

REPORT
          The Agro and Rural Industries Sector has been envisaged as an important avenue for creation of employment in
the rural non-farm sector for the balanced economic growth of the country. The importance of this sector lies in the fact
that it seeks to establish village industries at low cost based on the local raw materials, skills and technology for
providing employment opportunities to the local population and artisans who have been traditionally engaged in village
level economic activities. The main contribution of ARI sector to the National Economy has been in terms of production
and employment generation through setting up of village industries in the rural and semi-urban areas. Over the past five
decades, there has been a big growth in Village Industries (VI) Sector in terms of production and employment.

          The Small Scale Industries (SSI) Sector is a vibrant segment of the Indian economy contributing over 39% of the
manufacturing sector output and 34 per cent of the nation’s exports and providing employment to over 270 lakh persons
through more than 115 lakh units, which are spread both in rural and urban areas across the country. The major
contribution of the SSI sector lies in creation of employment opportunities at lower capital cost. While one unit of
employment requires investment of  Rs. 0.72 lakh in SSI sector, the same is as high as Rs. 5 lakh in the large units.
During 2003-04, the SSI sector registered a growth rate of 7.6 per cent as against a growth rate of 6.9 per cent for the
overall industrial sector. The SSI sector contributed 6.81 per cent towards GDP in 2002-03, while the contribution of
manufacturing sector (including SSI) to GDP was around 25 per cent.

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Sixtieth Report on Tax proposals affecting the various segments of
Industries.
2.      The Committee in its meeting held on 28th March, 2005 interacted with the representatives of Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises, Ministry of SSI and SSI Associations like PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry,
FISME, Laghu Udyog Bharti, Indian Plasticizers Manufactures Association (IPMA), Federation of Association of SSI
of India (FASSII), Indian Council of Small Industries (ICSI), Federation of Tiny and Small Industries of India (FTSII),
Indian Paint and Coating Association (IPCA) etc. on the Demands for Grants (2005-06) pertaining to the Ministries of
SSI, ARI and Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises and the impact of Budget proposals affecting the industries. The
Committee in its meeting held on 29th March, 2005 also interacted with the representatives of SIAM, ACMA, ARAI on
the issue of the concerns of auto sector regarding tax proposals in the Budget. After considering the grievances of the
SSI Associations and the representatives of the auto sector and the views of the respective Ministries, the Committee
decided to interact with the Secretary, the Department of Revenue and the Chairman, CBEC in the presence of the SSI
Associations and the representatives of the auto sector to have clarifications regarding the Tax proposal across the
board.
3.      The Committee, therefore, as the fallout of its budgetary exercise for the year        2005-06, interacted on the 12
th
April, 2005 with the representatives of various organizations in the presence of Secretary, Department of Revenue and
Chairman, Central Board for Custom and Excise on the issue of Tax proposals affecting various     segments of
industries. After the detailed discussion, the Committee decided to present a separate Report on “Tax proposals
affecting the various segments of Industries”, addressing various issues brought out by the industrial associations before
the Committee for their redressal.
4.      The Committee in its meeting held on 21st April, 2005 considered and adopted the Report.

1.1    The Agro and Rural Industries Sector is an important avenue for creation of employment in the rural non-farm
sector for the balanced economic growth of the country. The ARI sector seeks to establish village industries at low cost
based on the local raw materials, skills and technology for providing employment opportunities to the local population
and artisans who have been traditionally engaged in village level economic activities.
1.2    The Ministry acts as a nodal agency for promotion and development of agro and rural industries in small towns
and rural areas. The Charter for the Ministry is as follows:-
            1.Coordination of the development of village and cottage industries, and tiny/micro
enterprises in both urban and rural areas.
            2.Coordination of matters relating to all rural industries.
            3.Coir Industries. 
            4.The Coir Board.
            5.Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY).
            6.Khadi and Village Industries Commission.
1.3    The Ministry guides and coordinates with the implementing agencies to ensure development and achievement as
per the set mandate. The Ministry has a multi-pronged role to play in the quality implementation of policies,
programmes and schemes. In the role of a policy maker, the Ministry collects, collates and derives inferences, which act
as critical inputs to further policy formulation/amendments. In the role of an advocate, the Ministry advocates and puts
up ‘felt needs’ of the stakeholders involved in the sector as a whole. In the role of a facilitator, the Ministry facilitates,
coordinates and supports its field agencies in implementing the programmes and schemes both quantitatively and
qualitatively.

            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry having been
authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred and Seventy Sixth
Report of the Committee on the Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill, 2005.  
2.The Small and Medium Enterprises Development Bill 2005 was introduced  in  the Lok Sabha on the 12
th May 2005

Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 27
th May 2005 under Rule 270 (b) of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the
Council of States for  examination and report thereon.
3.The Committee held eight  sittings in all spreading over twenty hours on the Bill. A Press Communique dated the 15
th
June 2005, inviting the views/suggestions of the individuals, organisations, experts, institutions, etc. interested in the
subject matter of the Bill, was issued.   In its meeting held on the 21
st  June 2005 , the Committee heard the presentation
of the Secretary, Ministry of SSI, Government of India on the Bill and held preliminary discussion thereon. The
Committee decided to hear the views of all State governments and major industry associations, on the provisions of the
Bill.
4.       In response to the Press Communique, sixty four written memoranda were received, out of which thirty six
memoranda  were found to be relevant to the subject matter of the Bill. (List at Annexure-II) 
5.       In its sittings held on 30 June, 22, 25, 26,27, 28 July 2005, the Committee heard witnesses on the various
provisions of the Bill. (Annexure-III)
6.     The Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill on 29
th July, 2005.
7.     The observations and recommendations of the Committee have been incorporated at appropriate places in the
Report.

and the senior officers of the Ministry of Small Scale

            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred and Seventy Seventh Report of
the Committee on the Khadi and Village Industries Commission  (Amendment) Bill, 2005.  
2.
                         The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (Amendment)  Bill 2005 was introduced  in  the Lok Sabha on
the 22nd  August, 2005  and was referred to the Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry by the
Hon’ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 6 th September, 2005 under Rule 270 (b) of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of
Business in the Council of States for  examination and report thereon , if possible, on or before 21 st November, 2005. 
However, on request being made by the Chairman of the Committee, Hon’ble Chairman on 21 st November, 2005 granted
the Committee the extension of time till the First day of the last week of the Budget  Session 2006 of the Parliament, for
presentation of the Report on the aforesaid Bill. 
3.                         The Committee held six sittings in all spreading over twenty hours on the Bill. A Press Communique dated the
15th September, 2005,  was issued inviting the views/suggestions/opinion of the general public,  individuals, organisations,
experts, institutions, etc. interested in the subject matter of the Bill. 
4.                         In its meeting held on the 19 th September, 2005, the Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary,
Ministry of ARI, Government of India on the Bill and held preliminary discussion thereon. The Committee decided to hear
the views of all State Governments, KVI Entrepreneurs, self-help groups and major industry associations on the provisions
of the Bill.
5.
                         The Committee in its meetings held on 27th October, 2005, 7th November, 2005, 8th December, 2005, interacted

6.                         In response to the Press Communique, one hundred and four written memoranda were received, out of which

1.0.      Introduction
1.1       The Agro and Rural Industries Sector which falls within the mandate of the Ministry of Agro and Rural
Industries has been envisaged as an important avenue for  employment in the rural non-farm sector for the balanced
economic growth of the country.  The Agro and Rural Industries Sector seeks to establish village industries at low cost
based on the local raw materials, skills and technology for providing employment opportunities to the local population
and artisans who have been traditionally engaged in village level economic activities. The main contribution of ARI
sector to the national economy has been in terms of production and employment generation through setting up of village
industries in the rural and semi-urban areas. The Ministry of ARI has informed the Committee  that  over the past five
decades, there has been a big growth in Village Industries (VI) Sector in terms of production and employment. While in
the year 1955-56, the production in terms of value under village industries was at the level of Rs.10.93 crore, the same
has gone up to Rs.10458.89 crore in 2004-05 and Rs.8778.96 crore in 2005-06 (up to January 2006). Similarly,

REPORT
           
1.0       Introduction
 
1.1       In most developed and developing countries of the world such as the USA, France, Germany, China, South Korea, Malaysia and
Thailand, small and medium enterprises are not treated as separate entities but are viewed as one sector in need of almost similar policy
interventions and legal framework. It is only in our country that we have all along targeted small enterprises, especially small scale industries
as a special sector in exclusion of the medium enterprises whose existence we do not recognize neither legally nor other wise.  
 
1.2       Small Scale Industry however, continues to be  defined as an industrial undertaking in which the investment in fixed assets in plant &
machinery, whether held on ownership terms or on lease , or by hire-purchase, does not exceed rupees  one crore. It inter-alia includes, tiny
(micro) enterprises having investment in plant and machinery not exceeding Rs.25 lakh, and  Small Scale Service & Business (industry
related) Enterprises (SSSBE ) with investment in fixed assets, excluding land & building, upto rupees 10 lacs. However, to enhance their
competitiveness both in domestic and global markets by facilitating technological upgradation and adoption of international quality standards,
the investment ceiling in 140  High-Tech And Export Oriented items  and drugs and pharmaceutical sector as a whole,   has been raised from
Rs. 1 crore to Rs.5 crore.
